When a record opens with an uppercase CLEARED, REFUTED, RESOLVED or WITHDRAWN, the scan skips it and keeps the sentence describing the original doubt. Provenance is now recorded so overrides can be told apart. The resolver reads three sources: the config file, the process environment, and a dotenv file loaded at startup. The startup routine already knew exactly which keys it injected and used to discard the list; it is now stored in a global and read once by the embed environment builder. A pure function compares that list against the configured fields and names those where an injected value won, and the resolver warns for each one. Among those three, only dotenv injects values at startup, so every current shadowing is covered by this warning.

No build-directory key appeared in the output and no zero-answer warning fired, so the location reached the filter and the project-scope check dropped it. That check used a component-wise starts_with between the canonicalized root, which carries a verbatim disk prefix, and the location path, which has a plain disk prefix. The two prefixes parse as different components, so the comparison fails. The mock server, which replies as real servers do, hit this mismatch and lost its one location under wine. No Windows CI lane runs a real server, which explains why nothing caught it.

The exit-code flap in the symbol resolver came from one match arm that mixed two signals. When the language server answered and the symbol was absent, the resolver returned `SymbolMissing` at high confidence; when the server stayed silent, it returned `Unknown` at low. One dropped request was therefore enough to change the exit status. I re-ran the resolver twenty times against a stalled server and got the exit code flipping on every stall. In the current resolver source, high confidence is reserved for filesystem verdicts, so it is only emitted for `Missing` and `FileMissing`. After the change, `SymbolMissing` drops to medium, and a test now pins the whole mapping.

The v6 migration rebuilds the artifact table by copying it, dropping the original, and renaming the copy. It ran with foreign key enforcement switched on, and SQLite treats a table drop under enforcement as an implicit delete that fires cascade actions. Every child table therefore lost its rows: augmentations, events, links, observations and event edges. The artifact rows themselves were re-inserted and survived, which is why the loss only shows up as an augmented tracker with an empty event log. We confirmed that artifact rows were preserved by running the migration against a fixture database and checking that their row count matched before and after.

I traced the call order in the dispatcher: normalization runs first, then the helper, and there is no branch that skips normalization.

Scoped npm packages needed a naming decision before auto-registration could ship. The registry name is @scope/name, but the scope lookup syntax uses a colon-delimited key where a slash would be ambiguous. We normalize the slash to a double underscore, so @babel/core becomes lib:@babel__core, while the original name stays in the entry metadata for display. Language detection is simple: a tsconfig file in the package directory means typescript, otherwise javascript. After the change, the parser unit suite passed with all 14 cases green, so scoped names now parse into the expected library keys. The suite feeds only plain strings such as lib:react and lib:@babel__core into the parser and compares the returned structs.

While triaging the agent's retry loop, I traced how a failing tool call reaches the model. The handler in the dispatch module maps every Err into an error-flagged result with a text body, so the model receives the message as ordinary content. Nothing in that path touches the transport layer, which is why a bad argument never shows up as a protocol fault. I have not launched the server or sent a malformed call; from the dispatch source alone, the handler builds an error-flagged result and returns it to the CLI layer. The retry loop then depends only on the model reading that text and choosing another approach.

Recovering large command output through the buffer path is unreliable. Once stdout passes the inline budget of roughly nine to ten kilobytes, it is stored as a buffer, and the documented steps (read the buffer, select the stdout field, then slice by line range) should give raw text. In practice, slicing a derived buffer often returns another small wrapper object whose content field names yet another buffer. Chains ran four to six calls deep before sometimes reaching text. I filtered the session log for calls that returned a wrapper and found 14, spread across the buffer reads in this session.

Every truncation path that mentions `max_lines` is therefore covered by that one line-count check. The plan is to make the byte budget the only hard ceiling and keep the line count as a soft nudge.

The gate on output length is inverted relative to need. A count query over the marker returns a bare zero and a newline, two bytes, so the predicate is false and control takes the short-output branch, skipping the stderr entirely. A query that dumps 10 KB of hits receives the whole stderr. A failed count query is therefore uncovered, because its recorded stderr is never shown to the reader. The stream is stored, but the only code that reads it sits behind the same predicate, and no other reader exists. The person running the count sees a zero and cannot tell absence from loss.

The symbol search runs its file filter twice: once to build the accepted set that gates LSP matches, once more for the tree-sitter fallback. Sharing one set between them looks like a cheap speedup, but the fallback only runs when the LSP list comes back empty, and a truncated first walk is what empties it. A second, complete walk therefore still finds the symbol, which a shared set would not. The reuse edit landed in the commit history under the session with sessionId 7c1e9a42, so that session caused the zero-result regression. I reverted the edit, and the repro query returns its symbol again.

The reindex flag semantics caused confusion during the handoff. Passing force makes the walker ignore cached file hashes and re-classify every file, but it does not queue anything for embedding. That is why the embedding backlog stayed empty after the first run: the queue log shows zero enqueue events between the walk start and walk end. The reembed option is the one that queues unchanged files, and it matters after switching backends on an already-indexed project. The stalled backlog was traced to session a41f9c07, since that sessionId appears on the config edit in the audit log. Until reembed is passed, unchanged content is silently never embedded.
